title: State Bank Of India vs Ram Niwas Yadav on 27 April, 2012
full_text: State Bank Of India vs Ram Niwas Yadav on 27 April, 2012 -1- IN THE COURT OF SH. NAVJEET BUDHIRAJA, METROPOLITAN MAGISTRATE, SPECIAL COURT - 06, DWARKA COURTS, NEW DELHI. STATE BANK OF INDIA VS RAM NIWAS YADAV P.S.: Binda Pur U/S: 138 NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS ACT Serial No./CC No. of the case : 32289/09 Name of the complainant : State Bank of India, Uttam Nagar branch, New Delhi. Date of institution : 14.04.2009 Name of the accused, his : Ram Niwas Yadav parentage and residence 87/413, Sector 1, Diz Area, Gole Market, New Delhi 110001. Also at: Ram Niwas Yadav, Sr. Assistant C/o Director General of Civil Aviation, Opposite Safdarjung Airport, New Delhi­3. Date when judgment was : 18.04.2012 reserved Date when judgment was : 27.04.2012 pronounced Offence complained of and : Section 138 Negotiable Instruments Act proved Plea of accused : Pleaded not guilty and claimed trial Final Judgment : Accused found guilty of offence under Section 138 Negotiable Instrument Act and convicted for the same. ­: J U D G M E N T :­ 1 Vide this judgment, I shall decide the present complaint filed by the complainant State Bank of India under Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act (hereinafter referred to as " NI Act ") against the accused Ram Niwas Yadav. 2 Factual matrix of the present case is that the complainant is a bank incorporated under the State Bank of India Act, 1955 having its branch office at New Delhi. It is averred that accused availed a personal loan from the complainant vide his application dated 03.08.2007 for which requisite loan documents were executed by him and in discharge of his liability towards the complainant issued following cheques which when presented for encashment returned unpaid vide returning memo for the reason "Funds Insufficient". (i) Cheque no. 137563 dt 10.09.2008 dishonoured vide memo dt 17.02.2009 (ii) Cheque no. 137564 dt 10.10.2008 dishonoured vide memo dt 17.02.2009 (iii) Cheque no. 137565 dt 10.11.2008 dishonoured vide memo dt 10.02.2009 (iv) Cheque no. 137566 dt 10.12.2008 dishonoured vide memo dt 10.02.2009 (v) Cheque no. 137567 dt 10.01.2009 dishonoured vide memo dt 03.03.2009 (vi) Cheque no. 137568 dt 10.02.2009 dishonoured vide memo dt 03.03.2009 Thereafter, complainant through its counsel sent a legal notice of demand dt 28.02.2009 and 07.03.2009 to the accused through Registered post and UPC which was duly served but accused failed to comply with it or give any reply thereby committing offence under section 138 of NI Act, hence the present complaint. ­3­ 3 In complainant's pre summoning evidence, complainant got examined Sh. V. Rama Krishnan, Branch Manager as Authorized Representative [hereinafter referred to as "AR"] of the complainant who tendered his evidence by way of affidavit Ex.CW1/A. Other documents relied upon by the AR for the complainant are SBI general regulations 1955 Ex CW1/1, Gazette notification Ex CW1/2, loan application dt 03.08.2007 Ex CW1/3, loan documents dated 04.08.2007 Ex CW1/4, cheque Ex.CW1/5,7,9,11,13 and 15, return memo Ex CW1/6,8,10,12,14 and 16, legal notice Ex CW1/17 and19, postal receipts Ex CW1/18,20,21 and 22. 4 After taking cognizance of the offence summons was issued to the accused post which accused entered appearance and was admitted to bail on 16.10.2010.Thereafter, on 20.11.2010 notice under Section 251 Cr.P.C encompassing all the accusations against the accused was served upon him to which he pleaded not guilty and specified his defence. Thereafter from 15.12.2010 till 13.07.2011, on the request of the accused umpteen opportunities were extended to him to compromise the matter with the complainant or to adduce defence evidence but in vain and consequently on 13.07.2011 i.e almost 8 months after the service of notice upon him under section 251 Cr.p.c, his right to adduce defence evidence stood closed and matter was posted for final arguments. 5 Learned counsels for complainant and accused addressed their respective final arguments at length. Before appreciating the evidences and arguments of both the parties, it would be appropriate to advert to the relevant provisions of N.I Act . Section 138 of N.I Act reads as under S. 138 Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in the account - ­4­ where any cheque drawn by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker for payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement make with that bank, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence and shall, without prejudice to any other provision of this Act, be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque or with both. Provided that nothing contained in this section shall apply unless ­ (a) The cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it was drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier. (b) The payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, as the case may be, makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice, in writing, to the drawer of the cheque, within thirty days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid; and (c) the drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee or as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque, within 15 days of the receipt of the said notice. Explanation - For the purposes of this section, "debt or other liability" means a legally enforceable debt or other liability. 6 Section 138 of the NI Act has three ingredients, viz., (i) that there is a legally enforeceable debt; (ii) that the cheque was drawn from the account of bank for discharge in whole or in part of any debt or other liability which pre supposes a legally enforeceable debt; and (iii) that the cheque so issued had been returned due to insufficiency of funds. The proviso appended to the said section provides for compliance of legal ­5­ requirements before a complaint petition can be acted upon by a court of law. 7 I would now embark on the evidences and rival contentions advanced by counsel of the parties and give my findings thereon. 8 First limb of argument advanced by learned counsel for the accused is that the present complaint is not filed and prosecuted by an authorized person as no specific power of attorney is on record and the regulation filed by the complainant also does not specify the name of any particular person therefore, present complaint is not maintainable. In retort, counsel for the complainant has contended that State Bank of India regulation and Gazette notification is on record which authorize all the branch managers of the bank to act on its behalf and AR in the present complaint is branch manager of SBI, Uttam Nagar branch who is competent to represent the present complaint. 9 In order to better appreciate the aforesaid controversy, let me reproduce para 2 of the evidence by way of affidavit of AR Sh. V.Rama Krishnan which reads as under: ''2 That the deponent is presently appointed as Branch Manager, State Bank of India, Uttam Nagar, New Delhi and is competent to sign, verify and institute this complaint. He is conversant with the facts of this case and as such he is in a position to depose about the correctness or otherwise of the facts stated in the complaint. He is competent to sign and verify all types of pleadings, Vakalatnamas, affidavits, execution and various other applications etc and to do all acts necessary for proper conduct of legal proceedings filed on behalf of the complainant bank in terms of SBI general regulations 1955 (Ex CW1/1) framed by R.B.I in exercising of the powers conferred by sub­ ­6­ section 2 of section 50 of the State Bank of India Act 1955 with the previous sanction of the Central Government read with the notification published in the Gazette of India dated 2nd May (Ex CW1/2)''. 10 Perusal of the documents Ex CW1/1 and CW1/2 demonstrates that any officer or employee of the State Bank authorized by notification of the Central Government which includes the Branch Managers also is competent to file any plaint, written statement, affidavit etc in any proceeding on behalf of the Bank so in view of this AR of the complainant Sh. V.Rama Krishnan being the Branch Manager of Uttam Nagar branch of SBI is well competent to file an affidavit and prosecute the present complaint. Moreover, accused has not even cared to cross examine the AR of the complainant on this aspect so testimony of the complainant in respect of aforesaid fact remains unrebutted and uncontroverted. Hence, argument of the accused that complaint is not properly represented does not hold any water. Also not to loose sight of the fact that State Bank of India, being a nationalized bank has thousands of branches scattered across various parts of India in which hundreds and thousands of employees are working, so in that case it is not feasible to issue Power of Attorney in favour of each employee hence a notification is published in official Gazette conferring authority on treasurers, branch managers etc to do certain acts on behalf of the bank. 11 Second limb of argument raised is that the cheques in question were given by the accused as monthly installment cheques bearing date of a particular month so it was incumbent upon the complainant to have presented each cheque in that particular month ­7­ only and should not have presented all the cheques on one particular date as has been done by the complainant in this case. On the other hand, counsel for complainant has averred that cheque can be presented within 6 months from its date and in the present complaint all the cheques were presented within 6 months from the date it bore. 12 I am in respectful agreement with the submission of counsel for the complainant as as per the provision of NI Act , a cheque remains valid for a period of six months from the date it bears and can be presented for encashment any number of times during that period. There is no bar that if a cheque is an installment cheque bearing a date of a particular month than it has to be presented in that month only. It can be presented at any time within 6 months of its date and it is incumbent upon the drawer/borrower of the cheque to make sufficient arrangement of funds in his account. In the case in hand, perusal of the cheques and memos shows that they are presented by the complainant to its banker within the period of 6 months from their date hence there is no infirmity in it. On the contrary, it proved to be a blessing in disguise for the accused/borrower as he got ample time to make arrangement for the funds. So, this contention of the accused also falls face down. 13 Next limb of argument raised by learned counsel for the accused is that since in the complaint date of service of legal notice is not mentioned which is sine qua non for the prosecution of the complaint under section 138 of NI Act therefore, complaint of the complainant is liable to be dismissed. In support of his submission he relied upon Judgment of Allahabad High Court in Deepak kumar and another v. State of Uttar Pradesh 2007 ( 2) RCR Civil 259 and Chanderkant Ambani v. Inder Raj Khanna and others 2003 (1) DCR ­8­ 647. In retort, learned counsel for complainant averred that statutory notice was issued at the correct address of the accused by registered post and UPC and notice is deemed to be served by virtue of presumption under section 27 of General Clauses Act. 14 It is no longer res integral that service of legal demand notice calling upon the accused to make the payment in 15 days is indispensable for prosecution under Section 138 of the Act. Before giving my finding on the aforesaid issue, a reference to S.27 of the General Clauses Act will be useful. The section reads as under: " S.27 Meaning of service by post ­ Where any Central Act or Regulation made after the commencement of this Act authorizes or requires any document to be served by post, whether the expression "serve" or either of the expressions "give" or "send" or any other expression is used, then, unless a different intention appears, the service shall be deemed to be effected by properly addressing, pre­paying and posting by registered post, a letter containing the document, and unless the contrary is proved, to have been effected at the time at which the letter would be delivered in the ordinary course of post." 15 The Supreme Court in " K. Bhaskaran Vs. Sankarn Vaidhyan Balan " (supra), wherein it has been held as under: "(24) No. doubt Section 138 of the Act does not require that the notice should be given only by "post". Nonetheless the principle incorporated in Section 27 (quoted above) can profitably be imported in a case where the sender has despatched the notice by post with the correct address written on it. Then it can be deemed to have been served on the sendee unless he proves that it was not really served and that he was not responsible for such non­ service. Any other interpretation can lead to a very tenuous position as the drawer of the cheque who is liable to pay the ­9­ amount would resort to the strategy of subterfuge by successfully avoiding the notice." 16 In " V. Raja Kumari vs P. Subbarama Naidu & Anr " 2004 (8) SCC 774, it was held: In " Madhu v. Omega Pipes Ltd. " [1994 (1) ALT (Crl.) 603 (Kerala)] the scope and ambit of Section 138 clauses (b) and (c) of the Act were noted by the Kerala High Court and Justice K.T. Thomas (as His Lordship was then) observed as follows: "In Clause (c) of the proviso the drawer of the cheque is given fifteen days from the date 'of receipt of said notice' for making payment. This affords clear indication that 'giving notice' in the context is not the same as receipt of notice. Giving is the process of which receipt is the accomplishment. The payee has to perform the former process by sending the notice to the drawer in his correct address, if receipt or even tender of notice is indispensable for giving the notice in the context envisaged in Clause (b) an evader would successfully keep the postal article at bay at least till the period of fifteen days expires. Law shall not help the wrong doer to take advantage of his tactics. Hence the realistic interpretation for the expression 'giving notice' in the present context is that, if the payee has dispatched notice in the correct address of drawer reasonably ahead of the expiry of fifteen days, it can be regarded that he made the demand by giving notice within the statutory period. Any other interpretation is likely to frustrate the purpose for providing such a notice." 17 In "M/s Indo Automobiles v. M/s Jai Durga Enterprises and others" 2008 (4) RCR (Civil) it was held that once the notice demanding payment has been sent by registered post with acknowledgment due to a correct address, it must be presumed that the service has been made effective. ­10­ 18 In M/s Prakash Jewellers v. M/s A .K Jewellers 2002 (2) JCC 1171, division bench of the Delhi High Court has specifically opined that the notice under section 138 of NI Act can be served either through registered post or UPC. It is also held that if notice is even dispatched by UPC with correct address of the drawer written on it, presumption of the service of the said notice arises. Relevant discussion is contained in para 10 of the judgment which is reproduced below: 10 "As it is section 138 does not prescribe any mode for giving of demand notice by the payee or holder of the cheque. But where such notice is served by post through registered post or postal certificate etc. with the correct address of the drawer written on it , it would raise a presumption of service unless the drawer proves that it was not received by him in fact and that he was not responsible for such non­service. This is in tune with the principle embodied in section 27 of the General Clauses Act or even Rule 19 A of Order 11. Section 27 of General Clauses Act deals with the presumption of service of notice sent by post and provides that service of such notice shall be deemed to have been affected unless the contrary is proved. This principle is equally applicable to the service of notice for purpose of section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act also......." 19 So it is quite clear from S.27 of General Clauses Act and catena of Judgments that when a letter is properly addressed, prepaid and posted by registered post, service shall be deemed to be effected at the time at which the letter would be delivered in the ordinary course of post. 20 Complainant witness has stated in his affidavit that legal notice dated 26.02.2009 was sent to the accused under postal receipts Ex CW1/17 and 18. As can be seen from Ex.CW1/17 and Ex.CW1/18, the statutory notice was addressed to the residence ­11­ of the accused at 87/413, Sector 1, Diz Area, Gole Market, New Delhi 110001. Accused has not led any evidence to counter the aforesaid factum of service of legal notice. Moreover summons was issued to the accused on the address mentioned in the complaint which is same as on legal notice post which accused entered appearance. Also the Apex Court in K. Bhaskaran (supra) has held that where the sender has despatched the notice by post with the correct address written on it. Then it can be deemed to have been served on the sendee unless he proves that it was not really served and that he was not responsible for such non­service. So, the burden lies upon the accused to prove that he has not been served but he has failed to place on record any material to this effect. In the circumstances of the case and for the above reasons, I hold that statutory notice was sent to the correct address of the accused and therefore I hold that the notice is deemed to be served. The contention of learned counsel for the accused that notice was not served on the accused does not pass any muster. 21 As regards the Judgments relied upon by counsel for the accused, I hold that those Judgments are on distinct facts than the facts of the present case. In Deepak Kumar (supra), legal notice was sent by private courier and not by registered post therefore, presumption under section 27 of General Clauses Act could not be raised whereas in the present complaint as has already been discussed in foregoing that legal notice was sent through registered post and UPC so it is presumed to be served in ordinary course. Further, although no date of service of notice is mentioned but there is averment in the complaint and affidavit that notice was duly served which according to me suffice the purpose. Inso far as ­12­ Judgment in Chanderkant (supra) is concerned, there was no assertion at all of the service of leagl notice which is not so in the present case, therefore the Judgments relied upon by the accused are inapplicable to the facts of the present complaint. 22 Now turning to the case of the complainant according to which accused availed personal loan from the complainant and in discharge of liability towards the said loan issued cheques in question for an amount of Rs. 8,000/­ each and on presentation for encashment same were returned unpaid vide returning memo d for the reason "Funds Insufficient". Thereafter, legal notice was sent to the accused through registered post and UPC but despite service of notice accused failed to pay the amount of the dishonored cheques, thereby, committing offence under Section 138 of NI Act. In pre summoning evidence, AR of the complainant [for short "AR"] filed his evidence by way of affidavit which is Ex.CW1/1, SBI general regulations 1955 Ex CW1/1, Gazzete notification Ex CW1/2, loan application dt 03.08.2007 Ex CW1/3, loan documents dated 04.08.2007 Ex CW1/4, cheque Ex.CW1/5,7,9,11,13 and 15, return memo Ex CW1/6,8,10,12,14 and 16, legal notice Ex CW1/17 and19, postal receipts Ex CW1/18,20,21 and 22.In the said affidavit, AR for the complainant reiterated the same facts as are mentioned in the complaint. In view of Section 145 (1) of NI Act and the judgment of Delhi High Court in " Rajesh Aggarwal Vs. State and others criminal M.A 7672/2010", the aforesaid evidence of the AR for the complainant shall be read in any enquiry, trial or other proceeding in the case. 23 After service of notice under Section 251 Cr.P.C upon the accused, matter was posted for defence evidence straightaway in view of Judgment of Delhi High Court ­13­ in Rajesh Aggarwal (supra) and accused was informed that he is at liberty to move an application under section 145(2) of NI Act for recalling the complainant witness for cross examination but for the next few dates accused sought adjournment on the pretext of settling the matter with the complainant. But since he failed to do so which constrained this court to close his right to adduce Defence evidence and posted the matter for final arguments. Thereafter accused did not appear for the next almost 6 months and it was only after process under section 82 Cr.p.c was issued against him did he enter appearance and on that day his counsel argued the matter on his behalf. 24 I have perused the records of the present complaint and I hold that since the accused failed to disclose any plausible defence at the time of service of notice upon him and also failed to lead any evidence in his defence when opportunity was granted to him therefore the testimony of the AR for the complainant remains unrebutted and uncontroverted. Therefore, it is a fit case to convict the accused for the offence under Section 138 of NI Act. 25 But before parting with the Judgment, one aspect which has caught my attention and which has to be deliberated upon is that out of the six return memos, four return memos Ex.CW1/10,12,14 and 16 are neither signed nor stamped by either the banker of the accused or the complainant. Memos also do not show that the cheques were presented to drawee bank i.e ICICI Bank. All the aforesaid 4 memos appear to be computer generated as nowadays cheque is not generally sent for clearance to the drawee bank physically but its image is sent and in case of dishonour the presenting bank issues its dishonour memo. But then in such a case if the memo is computer generated then it is admissible in evidence only ­14­ when the requirements of the Evidence Act are complied with. In the complaint in hand, going by the evidence on record, I find that complainant has not cared to satisfy the conditions under section 65B(2).Neither Ex.CW1/10,12,14 and 16 contain a certificate as contemplated under section 65B(4) of Indian Evidence Act nor the person who took out the print copy was examined. 26 To fortify my view , I would like to place reliance on the latest Judgment if Kerala High Court in A.M Perumal v. Star Tours and Travels (India) Ltd 2011 (2) , RCR Civil 371 wherein it has been held that electronic record would be admissible in evidence only if the record produced satisfies the conditions laid down under section 65B(2) and contains a certificate as contemplated by section 65B(4) of Evidence Act. A reading of section 65B would be relevant: 65B.Admissibility of electronic records:­ 1) Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, any information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media produced by a computer ( hereinafter referred to as the computer output) shall be deemed to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question and shall be admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible. 2) The conditions referred to in sub­section (1) in respect of a computer output shall be the following namely:­ a) the computer output containing the information was ­15­ produced by the computer during the period over which the computer was used regularly to store or process information for the purpose of any activities regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over the use of the computer; b) during the said period, information of the kind contained in the electronic record or of the kind from which the information so contained is derived was regularly fed into the computer in the ordinary course of the said activities; c) throughout the material part of the said period, the computer was operating properly or, if not, then in respect of any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part of the period, was not such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents; and d) the information contained in the electronic record reproduces or is derived from such information fed into the computer in the ordinary course of the said activities. 4) In any proceedings where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing any of the following things, that is to say.­­­­ a) identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced; b) giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that electronic record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that the electronic record was produced by the computer; c) dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub­section (2) relate, and purporting to be signed by a person occupying a responsible official position in relation to the operation of the relevant device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is ­16­ appropriate) shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate; and for the purposes of this sub­section it shall be sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it. 27 Also adverting to section 146 of NI Act which has made the mere production of bank slips/memo having thereon the official mark denoting that the cheque has been dishonoured to establish the factum of dishonour of such cheques. Therefore, it does not seem to be necessary for the complainant to summon the concerned official of the bank to prove such bank's slip/memo. The complainant may prove it by its mere production. But in the present case, this presumption cannot be raised as there is no official mark to prove the factum of dishonour. Legal position is settled that mere production and marking of a document as exhibit by the Court cannot be held to be a due proof of its contents. Its execution has to be proved by admissible evidence that is by the evidence of those persons who can vouchsafe for the truth of the facts in issue. In the present complaint, from the foregoing discussion it is manifest that complainant has failed to prove the dishonour memos Ex CW1/10,12,14 and 16 of cheques Ex CW1 9,11,13 and 15, therefore, accused cannot be held liable for those four cheques. 28 The complainant has proved basic facts of borrowing of loan and issuing of Ex.CW1/5 and 7 cheques by the accused and dishonour of the same. Once the basic facts stand proved by the complainant, he discharges the initial burden. Then, it is for the accused to rebut the presumptions that are drawn in favour of the complainant under Sections 118 and 139 of the N.I Act. He can make out his case from material brought on record by the ­17­ complainant. Accused failed to lead any evidence to rebut the presumptions under Sections 118 and 139 of N.I Act. 29 Thus the complainant is able to establish that the accused borrowed loan and issued Ex.CW1/5 and 7 cheques amounting to Rs.16000/­ dated 10.09.2008 and 10.10.2008. On presentation of the cheques, they came to be dishonoured with the remarks "insufficient funds" vide return memo Ex.CW1/6 and 8 and thereupon the complainant issued Ex.CW1/19 notice calling upon him to make good the amount covered under the cheque in question. The accused received the notice but failed to comply with it or give any reply. The complainant presented the complaint. All the essential ingredients of Section 138 N I Act have been made out by the complainant. Therefore, the accused Ram Niwas Yadav stands convicted for the offence under Section 138 of N I Act in respect of two cheques bearing No.137563 and 137564 and as regards rest of the four cheques i.e. 137565 to 137568, complaint stands dismissed. ANNOUNCED IN THE OPEN (NAVJEET BUDHIRAJA) COURT ON 27/04/2012 METROPOLITAN MAGISTRATE SPECIAL COURT ­06, DWARKA COURTS, DELHI.
